name: Guam
summary_text: Guam stands under the full United States federal framework as an unincorporated United States territory. United States passports and other federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X gender marker was eliminated by a January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.  Screening at Guam's airport follows Transport Security Administration procedure, which applies in Guam as a United States territory. The agency's body-scanner and pat-down protocols can disclose a trans traveller's status to officers. Travellers may request an alternative screening method and escalate problems on the spot, and most trans travellers pass screening without incident. Guidance for trans travellers also addresses pre-flight packing and handling document and screening mismatches.  The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Guam, so access to that care during a visit can be constrained by federal policy rather than local practice.  A separate January 2025 executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly and directs the Secretary of Defense to submit an implementation plan within 30 days; the order frames trans identity as "radical gender ideology." It applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent United States military presence, and indicates the federal posture a visitor can expect from official institutions on the island.  On partner recognition, chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

Documents current surgery requirement for birth certificate/driver's license change.
sources.detail: No URL visible in provided text. Citation detail visible: introduced May 2018 by Sen. Fernando Esteves, defeated 6-7 on Dec 17, 2018; current rule requires physician sworn statement of sex reassignment surgery to Office of Vital Statistics / Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor.

name: Aceh
summary_text: Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and Aceh operates inside that national framework rather than alongside it. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.  Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.  Aceh is the only province in Indonesia operating a codified religious criminal law of its own, the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014). Same-sex conduct falls under the headings liwath and musahaqah.  Public caning is the standing punishment for sharia offences in Aceh. On 26 August 2025 two men were publicly caned in the provincial capital after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. Two men were also publicly caned in the province in February 2025 for a same-sex relationship.  Physical risk extends beyond the courts. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.  Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.  Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.  Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.  Documents and status are restrictive. Indonesia recognises only male and female sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

sources.detail: Cited as 'In 2005, the Indonesian government gave Aceh Province the right to introduce Sharia Law... punish anyone caught having gay sex with 100 lashes. The law was set for enforcement by the end of 2015.' No URL visible.
